meta.title: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper in Milan | Museum of Ages
meta.description: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper: a wall painting of 4.6 by 8.8 metres in a refectory in Milan, about 1494 to 1498. How it decayed, and what is left.
meta.og_title: Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper in Milan
meta.og_image_alt: The Last Supper drawn to one scale beside a person 1.7 metres tall: the wall painting is 4.6 by 8.8 metres. A drawing made for this page.

top.answer: The Last Supper is a wall painting by Leonardo da Vinci in the refectory, the dining hall, of the Dominican convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan. He painted it for Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, in about 1494 to 1498, and it is still on the wall he painted it on: 4.6 by 8.8 metres, height by width. Look under the table: Christ has no feet. In the seventeenth century the friars enlarged a door to the kitchens through the bottom of the wall, and the feet went with it.

blocks.h: How he painted it, and why it began to fail
paras: A wall painting of his time was usually a fresco: the painter works fast on wet plaster, and the colour is taken up by the wall as it dries. Leonardo did not want to work fast. The museum explains that he wanted to go slowly and change things as he went, so he painted on dry plaster instead, over a white ground, with tempera, the way he would paint a wooden panel. Lab studies find oil in the mix too. The paint sat on the wall instead of in it, and the room was damp. By 1517, within about twenty years, the painting was already flaking. In 1568 Vasari wrote that little could be made out beyond “a glowing stain”, as the museum's site quotes him.

The damage came in waves. In the seventeenth century the friars enlarged the door under the table (a catalogue dates it to 1652), and Christ's feet were lost. In the 1720s a restorer took the picture for an oil painting, the catalogue says, scrubbed it with caustic soda, varnished it with oil and repainted much of it. In the 1770s it was repainted again. In 1821 another restorer tried to peel parts of it off the wall. Under Napoleon the room was used by troops, as a stable by one account. Then the war. In August 1943 a bomb fell in the cloister beside the refectory and brought down its vault and its east wall. The painted wall stood. Since 1940 it had been shielded by a steel frame packed with sandbags, and that is what saved it. The room was rebuilt from 1945.

Restorers have been at the wall since the early 1700s, about nine times by the museum's count, and for most of that time restoring meant repainting what was missing. In the early 1900s Luigi Cavenaghi restored it, and in the 1950s Mauro Pellicioli secured the flaking surface without taking the old overpaint off. The last restoration was different. From the late 1970s to 1999, more than twenty years, Pinin Brambilla Barcilon worked across the whole wall, with the Milan Soprintendenza and the central restoration institute in Rome behind her, as the press reported at the time. Her team took off the overpaint of the earlier centuries, cleaned Leonardo's surviving paint flake by flake under magnification, as she described it, and toned the gaps in watercolour that can be washed off again. Earlier restorers, she reported, had moved eyes, closed mouths and added beards he never painted. What came back is thin. Experts' estimates of how much of the paint is Leonardo's own run from about a fifth to about a half. It is an estimate, and no single figure is agreed.

The painting is still in its room, which has been a World Heritage Site with the church and the convent since 1980. The air in the refectory is filtered and its climate is controlled, so you enter through a chain of small rooms whose doors open one after the other, and the visits are short, timed and in small groups. Booking is required. On the wall opposite is a Crucifixion by Giovanni Donato Montorfano, signed and dated 1495 and painted in true fresco. It has kept its colour far better than Leonardo's wall. Kneeling figures of the duke's family were added onto it, probably by Leonardo, the museum says, and of them almost nothing is left. For a visit, the museum's own site:

blocks.h: What our copy shows, and what it cannot
paras: In the museum's Leonardo wing a reproduction of the Last Supper fills a wall in the court, at the same 4.6 by 8.8 metres. It shows you two things a book cannot: the size, with you standing in front of it, and the whole composition at once, Christ in the middle and the apostles in four groups of three. It cannot show the wall itself: the surface of the plaster, the flakes and the toned gaps, the state the painting is really in. And it cannot show the room's light. In Milan the painted light falls from the left, like the daylight from the refectory's real windows. On any other wall that pairing is lost.
